items.title: eval: consider ClickHouse as primary store for billing analytics
items.body:
## Background

The current stack stores FOCUS 1.2 billing line items in PostgreSQL (`billing_line_items` table, 40+ columns, indexed on `billingPeriodStart/End`). This works for early development but PostgreSQL is an OLTP row-store — as billing data volumes grow into hundreds of millions or billions of rows, full-period aggregation queries will become the dominant performance bottleneck.

ClickHouse is a purpose-built columnar OLAP database with an Apache 2.0 licence that has become the de-facto standard for real-time billing and cost analytics at scale. Its design maps naturally to FOCUS billing data.

## Why ClickHouse fits FOCUS billing data

FOCUS 1.2 uses an **append-only correction model**: when a cloud provider discovers a billing error, it emits a new row with `ChargeClass = 'Correction'` — the original row is never mutated. This means billing data is structurally immutable from ingestion onward, which is a perfect fit for ClickHouse's MergeTree engine (which is designed for immutable sorted parts). ClickHouse's known weakness — expensive async mutations — is irrelevant for correction-model data.

Query patterns (aggregating `EffectiveCost` over time ranges, grouped by `ServiceName`, `ResourceId`, `Provider`, filtered by `BillingPeriod`) are exactly the columnar scan patterns ClickHouse is vectorised to execute.

Published benchmarks and real-world migrations show:
- 10–100x query latency reduction vs PostgreSQL on large billing datasets
- 10–30x storage compression (LZ4/ZSTD per-column codecs)
- Sub-second aggregations over billions of rows on modest hardware

## ClickHouse limitations to evaluate

- **Mutations are expensive and async.** `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` rewrites entire data parts in the background. No transactional consistency during mutation. This is a non-issue for billing data (append-only), but matters for any metadata co-located in ClickHouse.
- **Not suitable for OLTP.** User accounts, tenant configs, cost allocation rules, and workflow state require frequent updates and transactional guarantees — these must remain in PostgreSQL.
- **Operational complexity.** Self-hosting ClickHouse on Kubernetes (via the Altinity operator) requires managing ClickHouse Keeper (the ZooKeeper replacement), replication topology, and shard configuration. ClickHouse Cloud eliminates this at a cost premium.

## Recommended architecture: PostgreSQL + ClickHouse hybrid

| Data type | Store | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Billing line items (FOCUS) | ClickHouse | Columnar, analytical, append-only model, 10–100x query performance |
| App data (users, tenants, rules) | PostgreSQL (managed) | OLTP, full TypeORM/NestJS compatibility, CRUD/ACID |

The split is clean: the billing ingestion service writes directly to ClickHouse (dual-write, not routed through PostgreSQL). NestJS queries PostgreSQL for app state and ClickHouse for cost analytics via separate connection pools. No CDC or cross-system sync required for the core use case.

## Multi-tenancy in ClickHouse

Three patterns are supported; the recommended progression:

1. **Shared table with `tenant_id` in partition and primary key + ClickHouse row policies** — simplest to operate, good for early scale. Row policies transparently append `WHERE tenant_id = ...` at the database layer.
2. **Separate database per tenant** (`billing_acme`, `billing_globocorp`) — per-tenant TTL, partitioning, and data retention policies; clean GDPR deletion story (drop database). Suitable for large or regulated tenants.
3. **Separate cluster per tenant** — only for strict data residency requirements.

## Deployment options

- **ClickHouse Cloud** (recommended for early stage): managed, separated compute+storage, auto-pausing, no ZooKeeper/Keeper management. Note: 2025 pricing revision introduced egress fees — factor this into long-term cost modelling.
- **Altinity Kubernetes Operator** (v0.26, Apache 2.0): production-proven self-hosted K8s deployment, manages `ClickHouseInstallation` CRDs, rolling upgrades, replica management. Appropriate once the team has K8s DevOps capacity.

## Application integration

ClickHouse exposes an HTTP interface and a native TCP protocol. The `@clickhouse/client` Node.js SDK (official, maintained by ClickHouse Inc.) provides a typed query API. Billing queries are analytical SQL — TypeORM is not needed (and not appropriate) for ClickHouse; use the SDK directly in a `ClickHouseBillingRepository` service.

## Alternatives considered

- **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL extension with columnar compression and hypertables): viable up to ~100M rows with 10–100x query speedup over vanilla PostgreSQL. Simpler stack (one database). Does not close the performance gap for multi-billion-row datasets or sub-second interactive dashboards. Consider as a fallback if a single-database constraint is hard.
- **PostgreSQL with pg_partman + indexing**: reasonable for the current dataset; will not scale to the analytical query patterns expected in a production FinOps platform.

## Tasks

- [ ] Benchmark current PostgreSQL query performance on a representative billing dataset (1M, 100M rows)
- [ ] Evaluate ClickHouse Cloud vs self-hosted (Altinity operator) based on team capacity and cost
- [ ] Design ClickHouse schema for `billing_line_items` (partition by `toYYYYMM(billingPeriodStart)`, primary key `(tenant_id, billingPeriodStart, provider, serviceCategory)`)
- [ ] Implement `@clickhouse/client` adapter in billing ingestion service (replace/parallel to TypeORM insert)
- [ ] Implement ClickHouse row policies for tenant isolation (or per-database isolation if required)
- [ ] Migrate existing billing ingestion endpoint to write directly to ClickHouse
- [ ] Evaluate whether TimescaleDB is an acceptable interim step before committing to the hybrid stack
- [ ] Decide on multi-tenancy isolation level (shared table vs per-database) and document the decision

---
## Deutsche Fassung

## Hintergrund

Der aktuelle Stack speichert FOCUS-1.2-Abrechnungspositionen in PostgreSQL – Tabelle `billing_line_items` mit mehr als 40 Spalten und Indizes auf `billingPeriodStart/End`. Das funktioniert in der frühen Entwicklung, PostgreSQL ist jedoch ein zeilenorientierter OLTP-Speicher. Wenn das Abrechnungsvolumen auf Hunderte Millionen oder Milliarden Zeilen anwächst, werden Aggregationsabfragen über vollständige Perioden zum dominierenden Leistungsengpass.

ClickHouse ist eine speziell entwickelte spaltenorientierte OLAP-Datenbank unter Apache 2.0 und hat sich als De-facto-Standard für Echtzeit-Abrechnungs- und Kostenanalysen im großen Maßstab etabliert. Ihr Design passt natürlich zu FOCUS-Abrechnungsdaten.

## Warum ClickHouse zu FOCUS-Abrechnungsdaten passt

FOCUS 1.2 verwendet ein **Append-only-Korrekturmodell**: Entdeckt ein Cloud-Provider einen Abrechnungsfehler, erzeugt er eine neue Zeile mit `ChargeClass = 'Correction'`; die ursprüngliche Zeile wird nie verändert. Abrechnungsdaten sind damit ab der Datenübernahme strukturell unveränderlich – ideal für die MergeTree Engine von ClickHouse, die auf unveränderliche sortierte Teile ausgelegt ist. Die bekannte ClickHouse-Schwäche teurer asynchroner Mutationen spielt für dieses Korrekturmodell keine Rolle.

Abfragemuster wie die Aggregation von `EffectiveCost` über Zeiträume, gruppiert nach `ServiceName`, `ResourceId` oder `Provider` und gefiltert nach `BillingPeriod`, entsprechen genau den spaltenorientierten Scans, die ClickHouse vektorisiert ausführt.

Veröffentlichte Benchmarks und reale Migrationen zeigen:
- 10- bis 100-fach niedrigere Abfragelatenzen als PostgreSQL bei großen Abrechnungsdatensätzen,
- 10- bis 30-fache Speicherkompression durch spaltenspezifische LZ4-/ZSTD-Codecs,
- Aggregationen über Milliarden Zeilen in weniger als einer Sekunde auf moderater Hardware.

## Zu bewertende Einschränkungen von ClickHouse

- **Mutationen sind teuer und asynchron.** `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` schreibt ganze Datenteile im Hintergrund neu; währenddessen besteht keine transaktionale Konsistenz. Für Append-only-Abrechnungsdaten unproblematisch, aber relevant für gemeinsam gespeicherte Metadaten.
- **Nicht für OLTP geeignet.** Benutzerkonten, Mandantenkonfigurationen, Kostenverteilungsregeln und Workflow-Zustand benötigen häufige Updates und Transaktionsgarantien; sie müssen in PostgreSQL verbleiben.
- **Betriebliche Komplexität.** Selbst gehostetes ClickHouse auf Kubernetes mit Altinity Operator erfordert Verwaltung von ClickHouse Keeper, Replikationstopologie und Sharding. ClickHouse Cloud vermeidet dies gegen einen Preisaufschlag.

## Empfohlene Architektur: Hybrid aus PostgreSQL und ClickHouse

| Datentyp | Speicher | Begründung |
|---|---|---|
| Abrechnungspositionen – FOCUS | ClickHouse | spaltenorientiertes analytisches Append-only-Modell und 10- bis 100-fache Abfrageleistung |
| App-Daten – Benutzer, Mandanten, Regeln | verwaltetes PostgreSQL | OLTP, vollständige TypeORM-/NestJS-Kompatibilität und CRUD/ACID |

Die Trennung ist klar: Der Ingestion Service schreibt direkt nach ClickHouse – Dual Write, nicht über PostgreSQL. NestJS fragt PostgreSQL für App-Zustand und ClickHouse über getrennte Connection Pools für Kostenanalysen ab. Für den Kernanwendungsfall sind weder CDC noch systemübergreifende Synchronisierung erforderlich.

## Multi-Tenancy in ClickHouse

Drei unterstützte Muster mit empfohlener Entwicklung:

1. **Gemeinsame Tabelle mit `tenant_id` in Partition und Primärschlüssel sowie ClickHouse Row Policies:** einfachster Betrieb, gut für frühe Skalierung. Row Policies ergänzen auf Datenbankebene transparent `WHERE tenant_id = ...`.
2. **Eigene Datenbank pro Mandant** wie `billing_acme` oder `billing_globocorp`: mandantenspezifische TTL, Partitionierung und Aufbewahrung; saubere DSGVO-Löschung durch Löschen der Datenbank. Geeignet für große oder regulierte Mandanten.
3. **Eigener Cluster pro Mandant:** nur bei strikten Anforderungen an Datenresidenz.

## Deployment-Optionen

- **ClickHouse Cloud – für die Frühphase empfohlen:** verwaltet, getrennte Compute- und Storage-Ressourcen, Auto-Pause, keine Verwaltung von ZooKeeper oder Keeper. Die Preisänderung 2025 führte Egress-Gebühren ein; diese in langfristige Kostenmodelle einbeziehen.
- **Altinity Kubernetes Operator – Version 0.26, Apache 2.0:** produktionserprobtes selbst gehostetes K8s-Deployment mit Verwaltung von `ClickHouseInstallation`-CRDs, Rolling Upgrades und Replikaten. Sinnvoll, sobald das Team ausreichende K8s-DevOps-Kapazität besitzt.

## Anwendungsintegration

ClickHouse bietet HTTP und ein natives TCP-Protokoll. Das offizielle Node.js SDK `@clickhouse/client` stellt eine typisierte Query-API bereit. Abrechnungsabfragen sind analytisches SQL; TypeORM wird für ClickHouse weder benötigt noch empfohlen. Das SDK direkt in einem Service `ClickHouseBillingRepository` verwenden.

## Bewertete Alternativen

- **TimescaleDB:** PostgreSQL-Erweiterung mit spaltenorientierter Kompression und Hypertables; bis etwa 100 Millionen Zeilen tragfähig, mit 10- bis 100-facher Beschleunigung gegenüber einfachem PostgreSQL. Einfacherer Stack, aber bei Milliarden Zeilen oder interaktiven Dashboards unter einer Sekunde bleibt eine Leistungslücke. Als Rückfalloption bei harter Ein-Datenbank-Vorgabe erwägen.
- **PostgreSQL mit pg_partman und Indizes:** für den aktuellen Datensatz vernünftig, skaliert aber nicht auf die analytischen Abfragemuster einer produktiven FinOps-Plattform.

## Aufgaben

- [ ] Aktuelle PostgreSQL-Abfrageleistung mit repräsentativen Datensätzen von einer Million und 100 Millionen Zeilen benchmarken.
- [ ] ClickHouse Cloud und selbst gehosteten Altinity Operator anhand Teamkapazität und Kosten vergleichen.
- [ ] ClickHouse-Schema für `billing_line_items` entwerfen: Partition nach `toYYYYMM(billingPeriodStart)`, Primärschlüssel `(tenant_id, billingPeriodStart, provider, serviceCategory)`.
- [ ] Adapter mit `@clickhouse/client` im Ingestion Service implementieren – als Ersatz oder parallel zu TypeORM Insert.
- [ ] ClickHouse Row Policies für Mandantenisolation implementieren oder bei Bedarf Datenbanken trennen.
- [ ] Bestehenden Ingestion-Endpunkt auf direktes Schreiben nach ClickHouse migrieren.
- [ ] Bewerten, ob TimescaleDB als Zwischenschritt vor dem hybriden Stack akzeptabel ist.
- [ ] Isolationsniveau für Multi-Tenancy festlegen – gemeinsame Tabelle oder eigene Datenbank – und Entscheidung dokumentieren.

items.title: Phase 5 — Data Platform, BI, IA éducative et reporting institutionnel
items.body:
## Objectif
Transformer SchoolFlow Pro en plateforme data-driven : entrepôt analytique, tableaux de bord BI, indicateurs institutionnels, IA éducative, scoring étudiant, prédiction du décrochage, reporting ministère et pilotage stratégique.

Cette phase doit capitaliser sur les phases précédentes : production, sécurité, observabilité, SaaS, quotas et multi-tenant.

---

## Périmètre Phase 5

### 1. Data warehouse éducatif
- Créer une couche analytique séparée de l’OLTP opérationnel.
- Préparer schémas `bronze`, `silver`, `gold` ou équivalent.
- Construire des marts analytiques : élèves, inscriptions, présences, notes, finances, enseignants, campus, paiements.
- Prévoir refresh incrémental.
- Ne pas ralentir la base opérationnelle.

### 2. Modèle décisionnel BI
- Créer dimensions : date, tenant, campus, classe, niveau, programme, matière, enseignant, élève, parent, statut paiement.
- Créer faits : inscriptions, présences, notes, factures, paiements, absences, incidents, communications, connexions.
- Préparer modèle étoile compatible Superset/Metabase/Power BI.

### 3. Dashboards Superset / BI
- Dashboard direction établissement.
- Dashboard finance scolaire.
- Dashboard pédagogique.
- Dashboard présence/absentéisme.
- Dashboard multi-campus.
- Dashboard ministère / institution : indicateurs agrégés anonymisés.
- Dashboard SaaS platform usage si nécessaire.

### 4. Indicateurs clés éducatifs
- Taux de présence.
- Taux d’absentéisme.
- Moyenne par classe/matière/campus.
- Taux de réussite.
- Taux d’impayés.
- Recouvrement financier.
- Charge enseignants.
- Risque décrochage.
- Evolution inscriptions.
- Performance par période académique.

### 5. IA éducative
- Résumé automatique d’un élève.
- Recommandations pédagogiques.
- Détection d’élèves à risque.
- Aide à la rédaction de bulletins/commentaires.
- Assistant direction : synthèse activité établissement.
- Assistant parent : explication simple des notes/absences.
- Assistant enseignant : suggestions d’accompagnement.

### 6. ML prédictif
- Scoring risque décrochage.
- Scoring impayés.
- Prédiction absentéisme.
- Détection anomalies notes/paiements.
- Modèle simple au départ : règles + features SQL.
- Evolution future : scikit-learn / XGBoost / MLflow.

### 7. Gouvernance et confidentialité
- Anonymisation pour reporting institutionnel.
- Séparation données opérationnelles et analytiques.
- RLS analytique par tenant/campus/rôle.
- Masquage PII dans les vues ministère.
- Journalisation des exports BI.

### 8. Pipelines data
- Préparer jobs ETL/ELT async ou DBT.
- Option 1 : vues matérialisées PostgreSQL.
- Option 2 : dbt + PostgreSQL analytique.
- Option 3 futur : Airflow + warehouse séparé.
- Ajouter tests de qualité data : unicité, non-null, cohérence référentielle.

---

## Règles de sécurité
- Ne jamais exposer PII entre tenants.
- Les dashboards institutionnels doivent être anonymisés/agrégés.
- Les modèles IA ne doivent pas utiliser des données d’un tenant pour répondre à un autre tenant.
- Les exports doivent être journalisés.
- Toute vue analytique doit être filtrable par tenant ou explicitement globale/anonymisée.

---

## Découpage recommandé en PR

### PR 1 — Cadrage modèle analytique
- Ajouter `docs/data/ANALYTICS_MODEL.md`.
- Définir dimensions, faits, KPIs, règles de confidentialité.

### PR 2 — Vues analytiques PostgreSQL MVP
- Ajouter vues/matérialisées pour dashboard direction : élèves, présences, finances, notes.
- Ajouter migration non destructive.

### PR 3 — Data quality tests
- Ajouter tests SQL/pytest sur cohérence analytique.
- Vérifier tenant_id, dates, montants, statuts.

### PR 4 — Dashboard API analytics
- Ajouter endpoints API dashboard analytiques optimisés.
- Prévoir cache Redis court.

### PR 5 — Superset/BI pack
- Ajouter documentation connexion Superset.
- Ajouter datasets recommandés.
- Préparer export dashboard JSON si possible.

### PR 6 — IA éducative MVP
- Ajouter service de résumé élève.
- Ajouter garde-fous PII/tenant.
- Utiliser Groq/OpenRouter uniquement si clé configurée.

### PR 7 — Scoring risque décrochage V1
- Règles simples : absentéisme, baisse notes, impayés, retards.
- Score explicable, non bloquant.
- Dashboard alertes.

### PR 8 — Reporting institutionnel anonymisé
- Vues agrégées par région/campus/niveau/période.
- Pas de nom/prénom/email/téléphone.
- Documentation conformité.

---

## Critères d’acceptation
- Les données analytiques ne ralentissent pas les workflows opérationnels.
- Les KPIs direction sont disponibles avec cache ou vues optimisées.
- Les vues BI respectent le tenant isolation.
- Superset peut se connecter à un modèle propre sans requêter directement toutes les tables OLTP.
- Les premiers scores IA/ML sont explicables et non décisionnels.
- Le reporting institutionnel est anonymisé.
- Les exports analytiques sont traçables.

items.title: Tool checkout

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

Tools and test instruments are registered (#344) and their calibration is governed (#345), but nothing records who physically has an instrument. Engineering tool cribs in Indian hospitals run on a paper register or, more often, on nothing: a technician takes the earth-loop tester to the theatre block, a contractor borrows the pipe-threading set, and neither comes back. The observable consequences are an instrument that cannot be found when a P0 work order needs it, an instrument that silently misses its calibration despatch because it is in someone's bag, and an expensive instrument written off with no accountable holder.

Contractors make this materially worse. The platform grants contractors scoped access only — assigned facility, asset, work order, documents and time window — and that scoping means nothing if a contractor can walk out with a hospital-owned oxygen analyser and there is no custody record tying it to their induction and their permit window.

Affected roles: the tool-crib keeper (needs to know what is out and to whom), the maintenance and biomedical technicians (need to borrow quickly, often at night, without a keeper present), the biomedical engineer (cannot despatch an instrument for calibration that is in unknown hands), the contractor supervisor, and the facility manager who carries the asset loss. This is also NABH facility-management evidence: control of maintenance equipment is expected to be demonstrable.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** tool-crib keeper and maintenance technician
**I want** tools checked out to a named holder against a work order with an expected return time, and returned with a condition check
**So that** every instrument has an accountable custodian at all times and overdue items are chased before they are lost or miss calibration.

### Scope

**In scope**

* Checkout of a registered tool to a named holder (staff member or inducted contractor) against a work order or a stated purpose, with expected return date/time.
* Scan-to-checkout and scan-to-return from the FacilityConnect mobile app, working offline and reconciling on sync.
* Pre-checkout guards: tool must be `available`, in calibration if the intended work is calibration-sensitive (guard from #345), and the holder must be authorised for the tool's crib and, for contractors, hold a current induction and an in-window permit.
* Return capture: condition (`serviceable`, `damaged`, `needs_calibration`, `incomplete_kit`), optional photo evidence, and automatic state transition — `damaged` routes to `under_repair`, `needs_calibration` routes to `under_calibration`.
* Overdue detection with escalation to the holder, then the crib keeper, then the holder's supervisor, and finally a facility-manager loss review.
* Kit checkout: a named set of tools issued and returned as one unit, with per-item reconciliation on return so a missing item in a returned kit is detected.
* Custody handover between two staff members without a return to the crib, recorded as an explicit accepted transfer rather than an untracked pass-along.
* Crib dashboard: currently out, overdue, due back today, and per-holder outstanding items.

**Out of scope**

* The tool register, capability metadata and lifecycle states — #344.
* Calibration schedules, certificates and validity enforcement logic — #345; this issue calls that guard, it does not implement it.
* Consumable spare-part issue to a work order, which is a stock decrement and never returned — #343.
* PPE, which is issued as personal entitlement and generally not returned — #347.
* Contractor induction, permit-to-work approval and time-window definition — the permit-to-work and contractor-management stories in this epic; this issue consumes their state.
* Depreciation, insurance and asset write-off accounting — the finance module.

---

## Recommended Solution

Add a custody aggregate to `facility_inventory` (Go/Gin, GORM, PostgreSQL 16, RLS on `tenant_id`), with a Temporal workflow per open checkout driving the overdue escalation ladder. Temporal is the right fit because the escalation is a multi-step, multi-day, resumable timer chain with human interrupts (return, extension) — a cron sweep would either fire duplicates or lose state across deployments.

```sql
CREATE TABLE fc_tool_checkout (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, facility_id uuid NOT NULL,
  tool_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES fc_tool(id),
  kit_id uuid,                                    -- non-null when part of a kit issue
  holder_kind text NOT NULL CHECK (holder_kind IN ('staff','contractor')),
  holder_id uuid NOT NULL,
  work_order_id uuid, purpose text,
  issued_by uuid NOT NULL, issued_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  due_back_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  returned_at timestamptz, received_by uuid,
  return_condition text CHECK (return_condition IN
    ('serviceable','damaged','needs_calibration','incomplete_kit')),
  return_note text, return_photo_key text,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open'
    CHECK (status IN ('open','returned','transferred','written_off')),
  temporal_workflow_id text,
  idempotency_key text NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key),
  CHECK (due_back_at > issued_at),
  CHECK ((status = 'open') = (returned_at IS NULL)));

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX fc_tool_single_open_checkout
  ON fc_tool_checkout (tenant_id, tool_id) WHERE status = 'open';

CREATE TABLE fc_custody_transfer (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, checkout_id uuid NOT NULL,
  from_holder_id uuid NOT NULL, to_holder_id uuid NOT NULL,
  offered_at timestamptz NOT NULL, accepted_at timestamptz,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (status IN ('pending','accepted','declined','expired')));
```

`fc_tool_single_open_checkout` is the core integrity control: a partial unique index makes it structurally impossible for one physical instrument to be checked out to two people, which is exactly the failure that offline mobile clients would otherwise produce. Two technicians scanning the same tool in a basement plant room with no signal will both succeed locally; on sync the first write wins, the second returns `409 already_checked_out` naming the current holder, and the app surfaces a resolution prompt rather than silently discarding.

Checkout is a single transaction that inserts the checkout row, transitions the tool to `issued` via the #344 transition function, and starts the Temporal workflow. Guard evaluation runs before the transaction: tool state, calibration validity (`CalibrationGuard` from #345 when the work order's checklist is calibration-sensitive), OpenFGA holder check, and for contractors a check that the induction is current and the permit window covers `due_back_at`. A contractor's `due_back_at` is clamped to the end of their permit window — they cannot hold hospital equipment beyond their authorised time on site.

API surface (`/api/v1/facility`):

* `POST /tools/{id}/checkout`, `POST /tools/{id}/return`
* `POST /tool-kits/{id}/checkout`, `POST /tool-kits/{id}/return` (per-item reconciliation payload)
* `POST /checkouts/{id}/extend` — bounded extension with reason; contractors cannot extend past permit end
* `POST /checkouts/{id}/transfer`, `POST /custody-transfers/{id}/accept|decline`
* `GET /cribs/{store_id}/checkouts?status=open|overdue`
* `GET /holders/{id}/checkouts` — a technician's own outstanding items, the mobile home screen
* `POST /checkouts/{id}/write-off` — facility-manager only, closes an unrecoverable item

Events published: `facility.tool.checked_out.v1`, `facility.tool.returned.v1`, `facility.tool.checkout_overdue.v1`, `facility.tool.written_off.v1`. Consumed: `facility.workorder.closed.v1` (prompt the holder to return tools issued against it), `facility.calibration.due_soon.v1` (recall an instrument that is out and due for calibration), `facility.contractor.permit_closed.v1` (force an immediate return check before the contractor leaves site).

```json
{
  "event": "facility.tool.checkout_overdue.v1",
  "tenant_id": "…", "facility_id": "…",
  "checkout_id": "…", "tool_id": "…", "asset_tag": "BM-ELT-007",
  "holder_kind": "contractor", "holder_id": "…",
  "due_back_at": "2026-07-19T18:00:00+05:30", "overdue_hours": 26,
  "escalation_stage": "crib_keeper", "work_order_id": "WO-4620"
}
```

OpenFGA:

```
type tool_checkout
  relations
    define tool: [tool]
    define holder: [user]
    define can_checkout_self: user_of from tool
    define can_issue_to_other: keeper from tool
    define can_return: holder or keeper from tool
    define can_extend: holder or keeper from tool
    define can_write_off: facility_manager from tool
    define viewer: holder or keeper from tool
```

A technician may check a tool out to themselves (`can_checkout_self`) so an unattended night crib still works, but only a keeper may issue to a third party. Contractors are granted `user_of` on the crib only for the duration of their permit through a time-bounded tuple, so their checkout capability expires with their access rather than requiring manual revocation. Write-off is deliberately facility-manager only and always audited.

Sequencing: #344 (register and state machine) and #343 (crib as a store) must land first; #345 must land before the calibration guard on checkout can be enabled, though the rest of checkout can ship without it. Contractor induction and permit-to-work stories must land before contractor checkout is enabled — until then, contractor checkout is disabled by feature flag and a keeper issues on their behalf under their own accountability.

Risks: (1) offline double checkout — mitigated by the partial unique index plus idempotency key; (2) escalation spam from a legitimately long job — mitigated by bounded self-service extension with a reason before the ladder advances; (3) tools disappearing at the boundary of the calibration process — mitigated by the `calibration.due_soon` recall consumer, so an instrument out on loan is called back rather than quietly lapsing; (4) a holder leaving employment with items outstanding — mitigated by consuming the identity module's deactivation event to raise an immediate outstanding-items review to the facility manager.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** earth-loop tester `BM-ELT-007` is `available`, in calibration, and a technician is assigned to work order `WO-4620`
**When** the technician scans the tool's QR label on the mobile app and checks it out against `WO-4620` with a due-back time of 18:00 today
**Then** the tool state becomes `issued`, an open checkout is created naming the technician as holder, the tool disappears from crib availability, the escalation workflow is scheduled for 18:00, and `facility.tool.checked_out.v1` is published.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** two technicians working offline in a basement plant room both scan and check out multimeter `BM-MM-021` within the same minute
**When** their devices sync
**Then** exactly one open checkout exists, the first synced request succeeds, the second is rejected with `409 already_checked_out` naming the current holder and issue time, the second technician's local record is converted to a failed action with a clear prompt rather than being deleted, and the tool state is `issued` exactly once.

### Edge Cases

* A contractor attempts checkout with a permit expiring in two hours and requests a due-back of tomorrow — `due_back_at` is clamped to the permit end, the clamp is shown explicitly in the response, and any extension request beyond it is refused.
* A tool kit of six items is returned with five — return is accepted with condition `incomplete_kit`, the missing item stays `open` against the holder, and an exception is raised to the crib keeper.
* An instrument that is checked out becomes due for calibration — a recall notification is sent to the holder, the tool is flagged recall-pending in the crib view, and no new calibration-sensitive checkout can be created for it.
* A holder offers custody to a colleague who does not accept within the configured window — the transfer expires, custody remains with the original holder, and the escalation ladder is unaffected.
* A work order is closed while tools issued against it are still out — closure is permitted but the holder receives a return prompt and the checkout appears in an unreturned-after-closure list.
* A user with no relation to the crib calls `GET /cribs/{store_id}/checkouts` — denied with `403`; a cross-tenant call with a valid-looking `checkout_id` returns `404`, verified adversarially.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* Expected user or system outcome: every tool that leaves the crib has a named accountable holder, a due-back time and an automatic chase, and no instrument can be held by two people at once.
* Expected business or operational outcome: instrument loss and unavailability stop delaying critical work orders, and contractors cannot retain hospital equipment beyond their authorised site window.
* Success metric or validation method: ≥ 98% of checkouts returned or explicitly extended by their due time over a rolling 90 days; zero tools with more than one open checkout (nightly reconciliation query returns zero rows); tool write-offs reduced to under 1% of the crib per year; scan-to-checkout completes in ≤ 3 taps and p95 ≤ 400 ms online, with offline capture always succeeding locally.
* Monitoring period, where applicable: 90 days from go-live, reviewed monthly at the facilities operations meeting alongside the crib stock-take.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

None — all guardrails apply. The checkout and return journeys are primarily mobile, so accessibility must be validated on the Flutter app with screen-reader labels on the scan and condition controls, and a manual asset-tag entry path for technicians on devices without a usable camera.

items.title: Concurrent pipelines loading 2 datasets in 1 dataset share the staging dataset — merge silently duplicates or drops rows (ClickHouse)
items.body:
### dlt version
1.22.0 (`dlt[clickhouse,mssql]`), ClickHouse 26.5, Python 3.12

### Describe the problem

We run a multi-tenant ELT setup: **one pipeline per tenant** (~800 pipelines, `pipeline_name=f"sql_{tenant_id}"`), all loading into the **same dataset** so that all tenants land in shared destination tables (each row carries a `tenant_id` column; consumers rely on row policies). Tables use `write_disposition="merge"`. Pipelines run in parallel from an orchestrator (Dagster, one run per tenant).

Because the staging dataset name is derived from the dataset name (`staging_dataset_name_layout` default `"%s_staging"`), **every pipeline
shares the same physical staging tables**. dlt's merge assumes exclusive ownership of staging:
1. `TRUNCATE TABLE <staging>.<table>` at load start
2. `INSERT` the package's rows into staging
3. `DELETE FROM <target> WHERE _dlt_id IN (SELECT ... JOIN staging ...)`
4. `INSERT INTO <target> SELECT * FROM <staging>.<table>` — **no filter on
   `_dlt_load_id`**

With two pipelines overlapping on the same table, step 1 of pipeline B wipes pipeline A's staged-but-unmerged rows (silent row loss), and step 4 of  each pipeline copies *all* rows present in staging, including the other pipeline's (duplicates with identical `_dlt_id`).

### Observed

Two tenant pipelines started 0.8 s apart (fresh initial load of the same source shape). Result in the target table:
- 748 unique `_dlt_id`s per tenant, **1,496 stored rows per tenant** — every row inserted exactly twice, once by each pipeline's merge step (what we want).
- The next run (the update/incremental load), when 1 line is added to both source tables, the `_staging__` table got duplicate values since both contain the same `primary_key` but for different tenants.
- In an earlier overlap, one tenant's rows were silently lost instead (truncated from staging between insert and merge), which is worse: the incremental watermark had advanced, so the loss was permanent.

ClickHouse `system.query_log` confirms the interleaving (TRUNCATE from pipeline B between pipeline A's INSERT and merge, then two unfiltered
`INSERT INTO target SELECT ... FROM staging`).

### Reproduction

One pipeline per tenant (in production these are parallel orchestrator runs — Dagster partitions per tenant — here two threads with a barrier), dataset-less into the same ClickHouse database, both merging into one shared target table with a composite (tenant_id, id) primary key:

```python
import shutil, threading
from pathlib import Path

import clickhouse_connect
import dlt
from dlt.destinations.impl.clickhouse.clickhouse import ClickHouseClient

DB, ROWS, ATTEMPTS = "dlt_race_repro", 50_000, 5

# Mitigation we already run in production for a *separate* concurrency defect:
# dlt emits bare CREATE TABLE for data tables, so two pipelines creating the
# same shared table collide with "Code: 57 Table already exists" (without this
# patch, the repro corrupts via that DDL race on attempt 1 instead — one
# tenant's whole load errors out and is lost). With it, the staging race remains.
_orig = ClickHouseClient._make_create_table
def _ine(self, qualified_name, table):
    sql = _orig(self, qualified_name, table)
    return sql if "IF NOT EXISTS" in sql.upper() else sql.replace(
        "CREATE TABLE", "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS", 1)
ClickHouseClient._make_create_table = _ine

admin = clickhouse_connect.get_client(host="localhost", port=8123, username="default")
admin.command(f"CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS {DB}")
CREDS = {"host": "localhost", "port": 9000, "http_port": 8123,
         "username": "default", "password": "", "database": DB, "secure": 0}

def load(tenant, table, barrier):
    p = dlt.pipeline(pipeline_name=f"sql_{tenant}",
                     destination=dlt.destinations.clickhouse(credentials=CREDS))
    barrier.wait()  # start both loads simultaneously, like parallel partition runs
    p.run(({"id": i, "tenant_id": tenant, "payload": "x" * 64} for i in range(ROWS)),
          table_name=table, write_disposition="merge",
          primary_key=["tenant_id", "id"])

for attempt in range(1, ATTEMPTS + 1):
    table = f"t_{attempt}"
    for t in ("a", "b"):
        shutil.rmtree(Path.home() / ".dlt" / "pipelines" / f"sql_{t}",
                      ignore_errors=True)
    barrier = threading.Barrier(2)
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=load, args=(t, table, barrier))
               for t in ("a", "b")]
    [t.start() for t in threads]; [t.join() for t in threads]
    for tenant, cnt, uniq in admin.query(
        f"SELECT tenant_id, count(), uniqExact(_dlt_id) FROM {DB}.`{table}` "
        "GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY tenant_id").result_rows:
        print(f"attempt {attempt} tenant={tenant}: rows={cnt} unique={uniq} "
              f"duplicated={cnt - uniq} missing={ROWS - uniq}")
```

Output on my machine (attempt 1 clean — the race is a timing window; attempt 2 hits it):

```
attempt 1 tenant=a: rows=50000  unique=50000 duplicated=0     missing=0
attempt 1 tenant=b: rows=50000  unique=50000 duplicated=0     missing=0
attempt 2 tenant=a: rows=100000 unique=50000 duplicated=50000 missing=0
attempt 2 tenant=b: rows=100000 unique=50000 duplicated=50000 missing=0
```

Every row stored exactly twice with an identical `_dlt_id` — both pipelines' merge steps copied the full shared staging table. Depending on the interleaving the same setup instead loses one pipeline's rows (staging truncated between its insert and merge). Isolation of the runs' filesystems doesn't matter (in production these are separate Kubernetes pods): the shared state is the staging tables in the destination itself.

### Questions

1. **Is "one dataset = one concurrent writer" the intended contract?**
We couldn't find it stated in the destination or merge documentation. The failure mode today is silent — concurrent loads complete successfully and corrupt the data (duplicate or missing rows), rather than raising an error.

2. **Is there a recommended pattern for N pipelines loading one shared dataset?** 
Our use case is multi-tenant analytics: hundreds of per-tenant pipelines writing the same destination tables, each row carrying a `tenant_id`.

3. Data tables are created with a bare `CREATE TABLE` (`IF NOT EXISTS` seems reserved for dlt's internal tables), so two pipelines racing to create the same new table fail with `Code: 57 … Table already exists` and the losing load is aborted. Should `IF NOT EXISTS` apply to data tables as well? We currently monkeypatch `ClickHouseClient._make_create_table` to widen it.

Thanks a lot!

items.title: [Note] AI Engineer
items.body:
## AI Engineer 能力地圖：Frame × 關鍵字

以下以每個 frame 作為領域；每個關鍵字一列，欄位固定為一句話理解、概念、技術、實作、情境、注意；「一句話理解」以 Full Stack 工程師熟悉的系統開發視角說明。

### Data Engineering

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETL / ELT | 像後端資料搬運管線：抽取資料、整理格式，再送進分析系統。 | 把來源資料可靠地送到分析層；ETL先轉換、ELT先落地再轉換。 | 批次/增量、CDC、schema evolution、Spark/dbt。 | 以Airflow排程、dbt轉換、資料品質檢查與重跑機制落地。 | 報表、數據同步、資料湖到倉庫。 | 避免全量重跑；處理重複、遲到資料、PII與schema變更。 |
| Data Warehouse | 專門給報表與分析查詢的集中式資料庫。 | 面向分析的集中式資料儲存，重視一致性與查詢效能。 | 星型模型、分區、columnar storage、OLAP。 | 建立raw/staging/mart分層與維度/事實表。 | BI、KPI、跨來源報表。 | 不要把交易庫直接當分析庫；控管成本與資料新鮮度。 |
| Data Lake / Lakehouse | 像大型物件儲存倉庫，但加上可查詢、版本與治理能力。 | 保留大量原始資料並兼顧治理與分析能力。 | Object storage、Parquet、Delta/Iceberg、schema-on-read。 | 以bronze/silver/gold分層，設定catalog、partition與compact。 | 半結構化資料、ML訓練、歷史留存。 | 小檔案與無治理會拖垮查詢；需管理版本、權限與生命週期。 |
| Streaming / Real-time | 把資料當事件即時處理，類似 WebSocket 或 queue consumer。 | 資料事件產生後即時處理，而非等待批次窗口。 | Kafka/PubSub、Flink/Spark Streaming、watermark、幂等。 | 設計topic/schema、consumer group、checkpoint與DLQ。 | 即時告警、推薦、即時儀表板。 | 至少一次不等於不重複；處理順序、背壓、遲到事件與重放。 |
| Data Modeling | 替資料設計可長期維護的 schema、關聯與統計口徑。 | 把業務實體、關係與指標轉成可查詢且可演進的結構。 | 正規化/反正規化、維度建模、SCD、data contract。 | 先定義grain，再建立主鍵、外鍵、指標與欄位字典。 | 跨團隊共用資料、報表與特徵。 | grain不清會造成重複計算；避免只為當下報表硬編模型。 |
| Data Quality & Governance | 替資料加上測試、ownership、權限與可追溯性。 | 確保資料正確、完整、及時、可追溯且有人負責。 | 契約測試、expectations、lineage、catalog、SLA。 | 在pipeline加入schema、null、範圍、freshness與異常告警。 | 重要報表、監管資料、ML輸入。 | 品質規則要可執行；告警過多會被忽略，需訂責任人與處置流程。 |
| Orchestration | 像 CI/CD workflow，負責安排資料任務的順序、重試與排程。 | 管理資料工作流的依賴、重試、排程與可觀測性。 | DAG、Airflow/Dagster、sensor、backfill、retry。 | 任務保持冪等，設定timeout、重試、依賴與失敗通知。 | 多步ETL、每日報表、模型pipeline。 | 不要把業務邏輯塞進排程器；避免隱性依賴與無限重試。 |

### RAG / LLM Application

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | 把 ingestion、搜尋、LLM 與 API 拆成有清楚邊界的服務。 | 定義RAG元件如何串接、資料流如何走，以及同步/非同步邊界。 | Retriever-generator pipeline、API gateway、cache、queue。 | 拆 ingestion、retrieval、generation、evaluation 與 serving。 | 企業知識問答、客服、文件搜尋。 | 先定義延遲、成本、權限與失敗降級，再選框架。 |
| Chunking | 把長文件切成模型搜尋得到、又看得懂的小段落。 | 把文件切成適合檢索與模型上下文的片段。 | 固定長度、語意切分、recursive splitter、overlap。 | 依標題/段落切分，保留metadata並用檢索指標調整大小。 | 長文件問答、規章與技術文件。 | 切太小失去上下文，切太大降低召回；不要切斷表格與程式碼。 |
| Embedding | 把文字轉成可比較相似度的數字向量。 | 將文字轉成向量，讓語意相近內容在向量空間靠近。 | Transformer embedding、cosine similarity、批次embedding。 | 固定模型與版本，建立向量索引並記錄embedding model。 | 語意搜尋、相似案例、RAG召回。 | 模型換版需重建索引；多語、領域詞與向量維度要驗證。 |
| Vector DB | 替 embedding 建索引，讓系統能快速做語意搜尋。 | 儲存與查詢向量及其metadata的資料庫。 | HNSW/IVF、ANN、top-k、filter、Qdrant/pgvector/Milvus。 | 建立collection、索引、metadata filter與刪除/更新流程。 | 大量文件的語意檢索。 | top-k不是品質保證；注意索引更新、租戶隔離與查詢成本。 |
| Metadata Filtering | 像 SQL WHERE，先用權限、租戶或日期縮小搜尋範圍。 | 先用結構化條件縮小可檢索範圍，再做語意搜尋。 | 欄位filter、ACL filter、tenant_id、時間/版本條件。 | 把權限與來源metadata寫入chunk，檢索時強制套用。 | 依部門、產品、日期、權限搜尋。 | filter不能由模型自由決定；缺metadata會造成越權或漏召回。 |
| Hybrid Search | 同時跑關鍵字搜尋和語意搜尋，再合併結果。 | 結合關鍵字精確匹配與向量語意匹配。 | BM25、dense retrieval、rank fusion、RRF。 | 並行查詢兩路召回後融合、去重並評估權重。 | 專有名詞、編號與自然語言混合查詢。 | 只用向量容易漏掉ID/術語；融合權重需用資料驗證。 |
| Reranker | 像搜尋結果的第二輪排序器，把真正相關的內容往前排。 | 對初步召回結果重新排序，提升前幾筆相關性。 | Cross-encoder、Cohere rerank、top-N reranking。 | 先取較大的candidate pool，再對前N筆重排。 | 召回很多但答案常不在前幾筆。 | 會增加延遲與成本；不要把reranker當作權限層。 |
| Query Rewriting | 把使用者模糊的問題改寫成更容易查到資料的查詢。 | 把模糊、口語或多輪問題改寫成更適合檢索的查詢。 | Query expansion、multi-query、HyDE、conversation rewrite。 | 保留原問題，產生候選查詢並記錄改寫結果。 | 追問、省略主詞、跨語言與複雜問題。 | 改寫可能改變原意；需防止注入與錯誤擴張。 |
| Evaluation | 像單元測試與回歸測試，但測的是 AI 回答品質。 | 用可重複的案例與指標衡量檢索和生成品質。 | Recall@k、MRR、faithfulness、answer relevancy、LLM judge。 | 建立golden set、版本化評測並在CI執行回歸測試。 | prompt、模型、chunk策略比較。 | 單一分數會掩蓋失敗類型；要分檢索、生成與安全評估。 |
| Faithfulness | 檢查答案是否真的有文件證據支持。 | 答案是否能被提供的上下文支持，而非模型自行捏造。 | Citation checking、NLI、LLM-as-judge、groundedness。 | 要求引用來源，逐句比對claim與context並設拒答門檻。 | 法規、客服、內部知識問答。 | 有引用不代表真的支持；避免把judge分數當絕對真值。 |
| Hallucination | 模型講得很像真的，但內容其實沒有依據。 | 模型產生與證據不符或不存在的內容。 | Grounding、temperature control、answer abstention、fact check。 | 無證據時拒答，輸出引用與信心，記錄錯誤案例回歸。 | 資料不完整或問題超出知識庫。 | 降低temperature無法根治；需改善召回與輸出驗證。 |
| Failure Modes | 列出系統會怎麼壞，並預先設計偵測、降級與復原。 | 系統在資料、檢索、模型、工具或網路異常下的失敗型態。 | Failure taxonomy、chaos test、timeout、retry、DLQ。 | 建立錯誤分類、fallback、告警與可重現測試案例。 | 上線前演練與事故分析。 | 只測happy path不夠；重試可能放大流量與費用。 |

### Agent

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Workflow | 像後端狀態機，把 Agent 任務拆成可控制的步驟。 | 把Agent任務拆成可追蹤、可重試、可控的步驟。 | State machine、DAG、LangGraph、workflow engine。 | 明確定義節點輸入輸出、轉移條件與終止條件。 | 多步研究、客服處理、資料操作。 | 避免讓模型自行決定所有流程；限制迴圈與最大步數。 |
| Tool Calling | 讓模型用結構化參數呼叫 API，而不是只產生文字。 | 讓模型以結構化參數呼叫外部工具完成工作。 | Function calling、JSON schema、tool registry。 | 驗證參數、套用權限、執行工具並把結果回傳模型。 | 查詢API、寄信、寫入資料庫。 | 工具呼叫等同權限操作；需白名單、審計與人工核准。 |
| State | 保存 Agent 做到哪裡、拿到什麼結果，以及下一步要做什麼。 | 保存Agent在多步任務中的上下文、結果與目前階段。 | State schema、checkpoint、短期/長期記憶。 | 用明確schema儲存狀態，支援重試、恢復與版本遷移。 | 長流程、多輪對話、非同步任務。 | 不要把所有對話無限塞進prompt；避免狀態污染與競態。 |
| Planning | 讓 Agent 先拆任務再執行，但每一步仍要驗證。 | 先決定子任務與執行順序，再逐步完成目標。 | ReAct、plan-and-execute、task decomposition。 | 限制計畫深度，逐步驗證工具結果並允許重新規劃。 | 研究、複合查詢、跨系統流程。 | 計畫不是事實；每一步都需驗證，並防止無限重新規劃。 |
| Guardrails | 像 middleware 與 policy layer，限制模型與工具能做什麼。 | 在輸入、工具、輸出各階段限制Agent可做的事。 | Policy engine、schema validation、content filter、allowlist。 | 建立前置/後置檢查，違規時拒絕、修正或轉人工。 | 高風險自動化、金融、客服。 | 只做輸出過濾不夠；工具層和資料層也要防護。 |
| Human-in-the-loop | 高風險動作先停住，交給人核准後才繼續。 | 在高風險或不確定步驟由人審核、接管或核准。 | Approval gate、confidence threshold、escalation。 | 設計待審佇列、審核理由、逾時與回滾流程。 | 付款、刪除、對外發信、敏感回答。 | 人工介入點要可量化；避免所有案件都卡在人工作業。 |
| Structured Output | 要求模型回傳符合 JSON Schema 的資料，方便程式接續處理。 | 要求模型輸出可被程式可靠解析的固定結構。 | JSON schema、Pydantic、constrained decoding。 | 解析後做schema與業務規則驗證，失敗則修復或重試。 | API回應、分類、工作流節點。 | 格式正確不代表內容正確；限制欄位長度與注入內容。 |
| Evaluation | 像單元測試與回歸測試，但測的是 AI 回答品質。 | 用可重複的案例與指標衡量檢索和生成品質。 | Recall@k、MRR、faithfulness、answer relevancy、LLM judge。 | 建立golden set、版本化評測並在CI執行回歸測試。 | prompt、模型、chunk策略比較。 | 單一分數會掩蓋失敗類型；要分檢索、生成與安全評估。 |

| Evaluation | 像單元測試與回歸測試，但測的是 AI 回答品質。 | 用可重複的案例與指標衡量檢索和生成品質。 | Recall@k、MRR、faithfulness、answer relevancy、LLM judge。 | 建立golden set、版本化評測並在CI執行回歸測試。 | prompt、模型、chunk策略比較。 | 單一分數會掩蓋失敗類型；要分檢索、生成與安全評估。 |
| LLM Judge | 用另一個模型依評分規則批改 AI 回答。 | 用另一個模型依評分規準評估回答品質。 | Rubric、pairwise judge、calibration、human agreement。 | 固定prompt與模型版本，抽樣人工複核並監控偏差。 | 大量離線回歸、主觀品質評估。 | judge有偏見與位置效應；不要只依賴單一judge。 |
| Golden Dataset | AI 版本的固定測試案例與標準答案。 | 代表真實使用情境、具標準答案或評分規準的固定案例集。 | Versioned dataset、stratified sampling、edge cases。 | 標記來源、難度、語言與失敗類型，納入CI與變更審查。 | 模型/提示詞版本比較。 | 資料過時會誤導；要避免資料洩漏與只收集簡單案例。 |
| Observability | 把 metrics、logs、traces 串起來，看懂線上系統發生什麼。 | 讓團隊知道系統發生什麼、品質如何、成本多少。 | Metrics、logs、traces、dashboards、alerts。 | 關聯request id、tenant、model、prompt版本與結果指標。 | 線上除錯、SLA與容量規劃。 | 避免記錄原始敏感prompt；指標需能對應行動。 |
| Tracing | 像 distributed tracing，追蹤一次 AI 請求經過的所有步驟。 | 追蹤一次請求跨模型、檢索、工具與服務的完整路徑。 | OpenTelemetry、span、trace ID、Langfuse/Phoenix。 | 每個節點建立span，記錄輸入輸出摘要、耗時、token與錯誤。 | 定位慢點、錯誤與幻覺來源。 | trace資料可能含機密；設採樣、遮罩、保留期限。 |

### Multi-tenant

| 關鍵字 | 一句話理解 | 概念 | 技術 | 實作 | 情境 | 注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Multi-tenant Architecture | 同一套後端服務多家公司，但每家的資料與資源必須隔離。 | 同一平台服務多個租戶，同時共享效率與隔離安全。 | Shared service、tenant context、quota、policy。 | 每個request注入tenant context，所有資料與快取操作強制帶租戶。 | SaaS型AI平台。 | 租戶邊界必須端到端驗證，不能只靠前端參數。 |
| Tenant Isolation | 確保任何查詢、快取、檔案與向量都不會跨租戶。 | 防止一個租戶讀寫另一個租戶的資料與資源。 | Logical/physical isolation、ACL、RLS、network policy。 | 在資料庫、快取、向量庫、物件儲存與日誌都套隔離。 | 共享基礎設施的SaaS。 | 要測越權與錯誤租戶context；背景任務也要帶tenant。 |
| Tenant ID | 像 request context 的主鍵，必須一路帶過 API、DB、queue 與 log。 | 識別請求所屬租戶並貫穿整個資料流。 | JWT claims、request context、composite key。 | 由可信身份來源取得，寫入資料表、trace、queue與cache key。 | 多租戶API與非同步工作。 | 不可信任使用者自行傳入的tenant_id；防止IDOR。 |
| Shared Database / Shared Schema | 所有租戶共用表，用 tenant_id 與 RLS 做隔離。 | 所有租戶共用資料庫與schema，以成本換取隔離複雜度。 | tenant_id、RLS、composite index、partition。 | 所有表加tenant_id，Repository層強制篩選並做隔離測試。 | 大量小租戶、成本敏感SaaS。 | 漏一個where就可能資料外洩；索引與熱租戶需特別處理。 |
| Database per Tenant | 每個租戶一個資料庫，隔離更強但維運成本更高。 | 每個租戶使用獨立資料庫，隔離與客製化較強。 | Database provisioning、migration orchestration、connection pool。 | 自動建立/升級/備份資料庫並管理租戶路由。 | 少量大型或合規租戶。 | 運維與連線成本高；migration與跨租戶分析更複雜。 |
| Row-Level Security | 讓資料庫本身強制每列資料能被哪個租戶看到。 | 由資料庫在每一列層級強制租戶存取政策。 | PostgreSQL RLS、session context、policy。 | 交易開始設定tenant context，並測試直接SQL與服務帳號路徑。 | 共享schema的強制隔離。 | 繞過RLS的管理連線很危險；政策需納入migration與測試。 |
| Tenant-aware API | API 從驗證到查詢都必須知道目前是哪個租戶。 | API在授權、資料查詢與回應中都理解租戶邊界。 | JWT、middleware、OPA、quota。 | middleware解析tenant，服務層拒絕不一致context並套用配額。 | 多租戶REST/GraphQL服務。 | 不要只在controller過濾；內部服務與webhook也要驗證。 |
| Multi-tenant Scaling | 避免單一大租戶吃光資源，並能依租戶分片、限流與擴容。 | 在租戶數、流量與資料量成長時維持隔離與效能。 | Quota、sharding、partition、autoscaling、noisy-neighbor control。 | 依租戶分片/限流，監控單租戶資源與升級路徑。 | SaaS成長與大型租戶加入。 | 平均容量會掩蓋熱租戶；需壓測最壞分布。 |

# Database Cheatsheet — Block 1

## SQL vs NoSQL — main differences

| Aspect | Relational (SQL) | Non-relational (NoSQL) |
|---|---|---|
| Data model | Tables with rows and columns; fixed schema | Documents, key-value, wide-column, or graph; flexible/schemaless |
| Schema | Defined upfront, enforced by the DB | Often per-record, evolves freely |
| Query language | Standard SQL | Vendor-specific (MongoDB query, CQL, Cypher…) |
| Joins | First-class, optimized | Usually avoided; denormalize instead |
| Transactions | Full ACID across multiple rows/tables | Often BASE (eventual consistency); ACID is per-document or limited |
| Scaling | Vertical first; horizontal is harder (sharding is non-trivial) | Designed for horizontal scaling across nodes |
| Consistency model | Strong consistency by default | Tunable; often eventual |
| Examples | PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server | MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis, DynamoDB, Neo4j |

## When relational DBMS is better
- Data is **highly structured** and relationships matter (orders → customers → products).
- You need **strong consistency and transactions** — money, inventory, bookings.
- **Complex queries**, aggregations, multi-table joins, reporting.
- Regulatory/audit needs (well-defined schema, constraints, referential integrity).
- Moderate, predictable scale where a single powerful node is enough.

## When NoSQL is preferable
- **Massive horizontal scale** or write throughput (logs, telemetry, IoT, social feeds).
- **Schema fluidity** — fields differ per record, evolve fast (CMS, product catalogs).
- **Document-shaped data** that's read/written as a whole (user profiles, sessions).
- **Specialized access patterns**: graph traversals (Neo4j), key lookups with sub-ms latency (Redis), time-series, wide-column reads (Cassandra).
- Geographically distributed systems where availability beats strict consistency (CAP trade-off).

---

## Main DB objects and their purpose

- **Table** — the primary storage unit. Rows = records, columns = attributes with types. This is where data actually lives.
- **View** — a named, stored SELECT query. Doesn't store data itself (unless materialized); presents a virtual table. Useful for hiding complexity, enforcing security (expose only some columns), and reusing query logic. *Materialized views* do cache results and need refreshing.
- **Index** — auxiliary structure (typically B-tree) that speeds up lookups, joins, and ORDER BY on indexed columns. Cost: slower writes and extra disk. Primary keys get an index automatically.
- **Sequence** — a monotonic number generator independent of any table. Used to produce surrogate primary keys (`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` in PostgreSQL is backed by a sequence). Safe under concurrency.
- **Trigger** — procedural code that fires automatically on `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` (before or after). Used for audit logging, derived columns, enforcing complex rules that constraints can't express. Use sparingly — hidden behavior is hard to debug.

Other common objects worth knowing: **schema** (namespace), **stored procedure / function**, **constraint** (see below), **synonym/alias**, **materialized view**.

---

## SQL constraints

Constraints are rules the DB enforces on column values to keep data **valid and consistent**. The DB rejects any operation that would violate them.

| Constraint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `PRIMARY KEY` | Uniquely identifies each row. Implies `NOT NULL` + `UNIQUE`. One per table. |
| `FOREIGN KEY` | Value must exist in another table's referenced column. Enforces referential integrity. |
| `UNIQUE` | All values in the column (or combination) must be distinct. NULLs are usually allowed and treated as distinct. |
| `NOT NULL` | Column must have a value — no NULLs allowed. |
| `CHECK` | A boolean expression must be true for every row (e.g. `CHECK (age >= 0)`). |
| `DEFAULT` | Provides a value when none is supplied on INSERT. Strictly speaking it's a column default, not a constraint, but it's grouped with them. |

### UNIQUE on multiple columns?
Yes. A **composite UNIQUE constraint** enforces uniqueness on the **combination** of columns, not on each individually.

```sql
CREATE TABLE enrollment (
    student_id INT,
    course_id  INT,
    semester   TEXT,
    UNIQUE (student_id, course_id, semester)
);
```
A student can appear many times, a course can appear many times, but the triple `(student, course, semester)` is unique. Same idea applies to composite `PRIMARY KEY` and composite `FOREIGN KEY`.

### What happens when a constraint is violated?
- The DB **raises an error** and **rejects the statement**.
- If the statement was inside a transaction, the transaction can be rolled back (entirely, or to a savepoint) — nothing partial gets committed.
- This is exactly the mechanism that **preserves consistency**: bad data never lands in the table. The DB is in a valid state before the statement and in a valid state after. Without constraints, the application would have to enforce every rule itself, and any forgotten check or buggy code path becomes silent data corruption.

---

## DB modeling — three levels

- **Conceptual** — high-level, business-facing. Entities and relationships, no technology. Usually an ER diagram. Audience: stakeholders.
- **Logical** — normalized structure with attributes, keys, data types in abstract terms. Still DBMS-agnostic. Resolves many-to-many into associative entities.
- **Physical** — actual DDL for a specific DBMS: exact types, indexes, partitions, storage parameters, constraints. This is what you run.

### Relationship types
- **One-to-one (1:1)** — rare; one row in A corresponds to at most one in B. Implemented with a FK that's also UNIQUE, or by merging the tables.
- **One-to-many (1:N)** — most common. Implemented by putting an FK on the "many" side. Example: one customer, many orders → `orders.customer_id` references `customers.id`.
- **Many-to-many (M:N)** — implemented via a **junction (associative / link) table** holding two FKs:

```sql
CREATE TABLE students (id INT PRIMARY KEY, ...);
CREATE TABLE courses  (id INT PRIMARY KEY, ...);

CREATE TABLE student_courses (
    student_id INT REFERENCES students(id),
    course_id  INT REFERENCES courses(id),
    enrolled_on DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
```
The junction table can also carry attributes about the relationship itself (`enrolled_on`, `grade`, etc.).

---

## Anomalies in DBMS

Anomalies are the problems that appear when a table is poorly designed (typically un-normalized, with redundant data):

- **Insert anomaly** — can't add a fact because other unrelated info is missing. Example: a `courses` table that also stores instructor data — you can't add a new instructor until they're assigned a course.
- **Update anomaly** — the same fact is stored in many rows; updating it in one place leaves the others inconsistent. Example: customer address repeated on every order row — change it once, and the other rows still hold the old value.
- **Delete anomaly** — removing a row accidentally erases unrelated facts. Example: deleting the last order for a customer also wipes out that customer's data if both are in the same row.

Normalization is the fix.

---

## Normalization — 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF

The point: split tables so each fact is stored **once**, in **one place**, and depends on **the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key**.

- **1NF — atomic values.** No repeating groups, no lists/arrays in a single cell, each row uniquely identifiable. Each column holds one indivisible value.
  - Bad: a `phones` column holding `"555-1, 555-2"`.
  - Good: a separate `phone` table, one row per number.

- **2NF — no partial dependencies.** Already 1NF, and every non-key attribute depends on the **whole** primary key (only relevant when the PK is composite).
  - In `order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name)`, `product_name` depends only on `product_id`, not on the full PK → move it to `products`.

- **3NF — no transitive dependencies.** Already 2NF, and non-key attributes depend **only on the key**, not on other non-key attributes.
  - In `employees(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name)`, `dept_name` depends on `dept_id`, which depends on `emp_id` (transitively) → move `dept_name` to a `departments` table.

- **BCNF — Boyce–Codd Normal Form.** Stricter 3NF: for every non-trivial functional dependency `X → Y`, `X` must be a superkey. Fixes edge cases where 3NF still allows redundancy because a non-key attribute determines part of a candidate key.

Higher forms (4NF, 5NF) exist but are rarely needed in practice.

### Normalization vs history tables
Tables that store **history or repeated interactions** (orders, events, audit logs, transactions, interlinear word-level data, OCR lines) look "redundant" at first glance, but **they're not redundancy — each row is a distinct event in time**, and normalization doesn't ask you to deduplicate them.

What changes:
- Keep the **descriptive** data (customer name, product name, department) in their own tables and reference them by FK from the history rows. The history table stays narrow and links out.
- But sometimes you **intentionally denormalize** historical data — e.g., store the **price at the time of sale** on the order line, because the product price will change later and you need the historical truth, not the current value. This is a deliberate choice, not a normalization failure.
- For analytical / OLAP workloads (think your `sh` sales schema with window functions), star/snowflake schemas deliberately denormalize for read performance. Fact tables = events, dimension tables = descriptions. Updates are rare, reads are heavy, so the trade-off flips.

Rule of thumb: normalize for OLTP (correctness, concurrent writes); denormalize selectively for OLAP (read speed) or for capturing point-in-time truth.

items.body: ### What happened? Opening a table with a large number of columns (~100) makes the data grid unusable on three fronts: 1. **Flickering** — as soon as the grid renders, cells/columns flicker continuously. It gets worse while scrolling right. 2. **Columns eventually stop loading** — after scrolling horizontally for a while, columns stop rendering entirely. Header cells and/or data cells come up blank and never recover; only reopening the table (sometimes restarting the app) brings them back. 3. **Horizontal scroll lags behind the actual scroll position** — scrolling left/right, the rendered content can't keep up with the scroll offset. There's a visible gap between the last painted column and the right edge of the viewport (empty background where columns should be), which fills in only after scrolling stops. Point 3 is what the screenshot below shows: scrolled right, the rightmost region ("Gap") is empty even though there are ~80 more columns after `ratio`. Vertical scrolling on the same table is fine — the problem is specific to column count / horizontal virtualization. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Create a table with ~100 columns of mixed types (script below). 2. Connect to it in TablePro (MySQL, local). 3. Open `wide_test_table` in the data grid → flickering starts after scrolling to the right. 4. Scroll horizontally, fast, left and right a few times → gap between painted columns and scroll position; after a while columns stop rendering at all. Repro schema (MySQL 8.0), 100 columns × 25 rows — mixed types incl. `JSON`, `ENUM`, `SET`, `BIT`, `BLOB`, `MEDIUMTEXT`, unicode/emoji and NULL-heavy columns: ```sql CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS items.title: Task: Collection detail + HTMX re-probe (readiness card swap) + confirm-gated enable/disable

labels.name: frontend
labels.description: Operator web UI — G10.x HTMX/Jinja console surface

items.body:
Parent goal: #336
Parent initiative: #1836

## Context

T1 (#1836 sibling) ships the admin Collections lifecycle **table** (a "Collections" tab on `/ui/corpus`, NOT entitlement-filtered) + the **register** modal. This Task (T2) completes the self-service loop: a per-collection **detail page**, an HTMX **re-probe** action (readiness-card swap), and **confirm-gated enable/disable** — then repoints the corpus empty state at the in-console register flow.

All backend surface exists and is stable (`backend/src/meho_backplane/api/v1/doc_collections.py`, the `docs_collections/` service + lifecycle state machine). This is pure UI/BFF assembly — **no backend work**. The chassis is the connectors detail + re-probe surface, which this Task reuses near-verbatim.

## Current state

- Three `tenant_admin`-gated lifecycle routes exist (`doc_collections.py`, `_require_admin = Depends(require_role(TenantRole.TENANT_ADMIN))`, `:97`):
  - `POST /api/v1/doc_collections/{collection_key}/probe` (`:287`, `probe_collection_endpoint`) → returns typed `BackendReadiness` on success (persists `readiness`/`doc_count`/`last_ingested_at`/`status`), maps a failed/unreachable backend to **503** (`CorpusUnavailable`, success-only write-back), **404** unknown key, **409** forbidden transition.
  - `POST /api/v1/doc_collections/{collection_key}/enable` (`:331`) → **204**, idempotent, 404/409.
  - `POST /api/v1/doc_collections/{collection_key}/disable` (`:357`) → **204**, idempotent, 404/409.
- In-process services to call (NOT the Bearer API): `probe_collection` (`docs_collections/service.py:216`), `set_collection_enabled(session, collection, *, enabled)` (`service.py:284`, returns `True` on actual change / `False` on idempotent no-op), `resolve_doc_collection(session, collection_key, tenant_id)` (`docs_collections/resolver.py:78`, tenant-first, raises `DocCollectionNotFoundError`).
- Lifecycle state machine (`docs_collections/lifecycle.py`): states `provisioning`/`ready`/`rebuilding`/`disabled`; `DocCollectionStateError` is an `HTTPException` **409** with `detail.error="invalid_collection_transition"` (`:118`). `disable` reachable from any live state; `enable` → `provisioning`.
- `BackendReadiness` (`docs_search/backends/base.py:57`): `reachable: bool`, `index_built: bool` (the managed-RAG footgun — reachable ≠ answerable), plus `doc_count`/`last_ingested_at`/`detail`.
- Connectors chassis to reuse verbatim (per the initiative's "Shared groundwork"): detail page `ui/routes/connectors/detail.py`; **re-probe** `ui/routes/connectors/probe.py` (HTMX `hx-post` + `hx-target="#fingerprint-card"` + `hx-swap="outerHTML"`, renders `connectors/_fingerprint_card.html` on success or `connectors/_probe_alert.html` on failure, gated by `resolve_operator_or_403`); **confirm modal** `connectors/_delete_modal.html` + `forms.py::render_delete_modal`/`submit_delete`; soft-hide `resolve_role_probe` (`operator.py:152`).
- `backend{type,ref}` is **server-side-only** — omitted from `DocCollectionSummary` (`schemas.py:189`, `#1548`) but present on the full `DocCollection` read shape (`schemas.py:131,156`). The initiative footgun: show `backend{type,ref}` **only on the tenant_admin detail page**.
- Versions: HTMX 2 + Alpine 3 (`ui/templates/_head_assets.html:35,37`); `fastapi>=0.136.3,<0.137`, `jinja2>=3.1.6` (`backend/pyproject.toml`).

## Scope

1. **Collection detail page.** Add `GET /ui/corpus/collections/{collection_key}` (linked from the T1 table row). Reconstruct the operator via `_resolve_operator` (`corpus/routes.py:136`); resolve the row tenant-first via `resolve_doc_collection` (`resolver.py:78`) → 404 on an unknown/cross-tenant key. Render the full `DocCollection` read shape (`project_doc_collection`, `schemas.py:219`): identity header (`collection_key`/`vendor`/`products`), a **readiness card** (`status` pill, `doc_count`, `last_ingested_at`, `readiness.index_built`), and — **only when `is_tenant_admin`** — the server-side-only `backend{type,ref}`. Use `resolve_role_probe` (`operator.py:152`) for the `is_tenant_admin` flag.

2. **HTMX re-probe (readiness card swap).** Add `POST /ui/corpus/collections/{collection_key}/probe`, `tenant_admin`-gated server-side via `resolve_operator_or_403` (`operator.py:184`). Call the in-process `probe_collection` service (`service.py:216`) inside an open transaction (mirror `doc_collections.py:287` — resolve then probe; a `CorpusUnavailable` rolls back and maps to a 503 alert). On success re-render the readiness card fragment and swap it (`hx-target="#collection-readiness-card"`, `hx-swap="outerHTML"`) — the exact `_fingerprint_card.html` swap pattern from `connectors/probe.py:_do_probe`. On 503/409 render an alert fragment (mirror `connectors/_probe_alert.html`) into the card slot.

3. **Probe is slow — pending state (load-bearing footgun).** A probe is a potentially-serialized remote call (per-project rebuild serialization). The re-probe button MUST use HTMX `hx-disabled-elt="this"` and a clear pending state (e.g. `hx-indicator`) so a naive synchronous HTMX probe does not look hung. Cite the in-repo connectors re-probe button as the convention.

4. **Confirm-gated enable/disable.** Add `GET /ui/corpus/collections/{collection_key}/disable` (HTMX-loaded confirm modal, `tenant_admin`-gated) mirroring `connectors/_delete_modal.html` — **disable is availability-destructive** (a disabled collection fails `search_docs` with terminal `403 collection_disabled` for ALL searchers, `doc_collections.py:357` docstring), so the modal must spell out that impact, like the connectors delete confirm. Add `POST /ui/corpus/collections/{collection_key}/disable` and a matching `enable` POST (enable is non-destructive → a plain confirmed button, no scary modal needed). Both call the in-process `set_collection_enabled` service (`service.py:284`); surface idempotent `204` (no-op returns `False` → "already disabled/enabled, nothing changed") and `DocCollectionStateError`→`409 invalid_collection_transition` legibly as an alert (not a stack trace). On success return `HX-Redirect` to the detail page (or swap the readiness card + action buttons).

5. **CSRF.** Every state-changing verb (probe/enable/disable) rides the double-submit `meho_csrf` cookie via `hx-headers` `X-CSRF-Token` (`ui/csrf.py`; HTMX does not propagate `hx-headers` to descendant forms — #1693 class). Mint + re-set the cookie on each modal/card render (mirror `connectors/probe.py:_do_probe`).

6. **Route ordering (load-bearing).** The new routes share the `/ui/corpus/collections/{collection_key}` param. Register the literal `/ui/corpus/collections/register` (from T1) and any other literal segment **before** the `{collection_key}` param route so first-match-wins never binds a literal as `collection_key`. The action sub-routes (`/{collection_key}/probe`, `/{collection_key}/disable`, `/{collection_key}/enable`) carry an extra literal segment so they are unambiguous, but keep the GET detail `{collection_key}` route registered after all literal-prefixed routes. Document it with a code comment (mirror `connectors/__init__.py::build_router`).

7. **Repoint the corpus empty state.** Change the `{% else %}` "ask an administrator to register and entitle a collection" block in `corpus/index.html` (the genuinely-unprovisioned arm) to link to the in-console register flow (the T1 register modal / Collections tab) for `tenant_admin` operators — closing the initiative's "Done when" ("the corpus empty state points to the in-console register flow instead of 'ask an administrator.'"). Keep the entitlement-diagnostic arm (`entitlement_diagnostic`, the missing-`meho-docs:<key>` case) unchanged — that is not a registration problem.

## Acceptance criteria

- A pytest test asserts `POST /ui/corpus/collections/{key}/probe` as `tenant_admin` against a reachable index re-renders the readiness card with `status=ready` and the new `doc_count` (swap target `#collection-readiness-card`); and that an unreachable backend yields a 503 alert fragment while the DB row's `status` is left unchanged (success-only write-back). (e.g. `backend/tests/test_ui_corpus_collection_detail.py::test_reprobe_card_swap_and_503`)
- A pytest test asserts `POST /ui/corpus/collections/{key}/disable` transitions the row to `disabled`, a second disable is the idempotent no-op (no error), and a forbidden transition surfaces `409 invalid_collection_transition` as a legible alert (not a 500). (`::test_disable_idempotent_and_409`)
- A pytest test asserts the detail page shows `backend{type,ref}` for a `tenant_admin` and **hides** it for a plain `operator` (grep the response HTML for the backend `ref` value presence/absence). (`::test_backend_ref_admin_only`)
- A pytest test asserts a non-`tenant_admin` crafted `POST .../probe` and `.../disable` both return 403 (server-side `resolve_operator_or_403` gate), and that the re-probe button carries `hx-disabled-elt` (grep the detail HTML). (`::test_probe_disable_403_and_pending_state`)
- A pytest test asserts route-ordering first-match-wins: a literal sub-route is NOT bound as `{collection_key}` — `GET /ui/corpus/collections/register` (the T1 literal) resolves to the register modal, not to the detail handler with `collection_key="register"`, and the action POSTs (`/{collection_key}/probe`, `/disable`, `/enable`) resolve to their literal-suffixed handlers. (`::test_literal_routes_not_shadowed_by_param`)
- `grep -n "register" backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/templates/corpus/index.html` shows the empty-state `{% else %}` unprovisioned arm now links to the in-console register flow, and `grep -c "ask an administrator to register and entitle a collection"` returns 0 (the old dead-end string is gone from the unprovisioned arm; the `entitlement_diagnostic` "Ask an administrator to grant" arm at `index.html:141` is intentionally unchanged).
- Run `cd cli && make snapshot-openapi && make generate` and commit the regenerated `cli/api/openapi.json` + `cli/internal/api/client.gen.go`; CI lane "CLI API snapshot freshness" passes. (The new `/ui/corpus/collections/{collection_key}*` routes register into the FastAPI app and land in the committed snapshot — the initiative's "No OpenAPI snapshot change" note is FALSE for route-adding tasks.)
- `uv run ruff check` and `uv run mypy` pass on the changed modules; the corpus UI test suite is green under `uv run pytest`.

## Out of scope

- The Collections table + register modal → T1 (#1836 sibling).
- PATCH/DELETE of a collection (no `DocCollectionUpdate` schema — `schemas.py:30`).
- Per-collection entitlement (`meho-docs:<key>`) grant UI — that is a Keycloak claim concern, not a lifecycle action.
- Bulk probe/enable/disable across collections.

## References

- Backend lifecycle routes (reuse via in-process service, NOT Bearer API): `backend/src/meho_backplane/api/v1/doc_collections.py:97,287,331,357` (admin gate, probe, enable, disable).
- In-process services: `backend/src/meho_backplane/docs_collections/service.py:216` (`probe_collection`), `:284` (`set_collection_enabled`); resolver `backend/src/meho_backplane/docs_collections/resolver.py:78` (`resolve_doc_collection`); lifecycle `backend/src/meho_backplane/docs_collections/lifecycle.py:118` (`DocCollectionStateError` → 409).
- Read shape + projection: `backend/src/meho_backplane/docs_collections/schemas.py:131,156,219` (`DocCollection`, `backend` field, `project_doc_collection`); `backend/src/meho_backplane/docs_search/backends/base.py:57` (`BackendReadiness`: `reachable`/`index_built`).
- Precedent UI chassis (convention authority): re-probe action `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/routes/connectors/probe.py` (`_do_probe`, card swap, alert fragment, CSRF re-set); detail page `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/routes/connectors/detail.py`; confirm modal `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/templates/connectors/_delete_modal.html` + `ui/routes/connectors/forms.py` (`render_delete_modal`/`submit_delete`); fragment templates `connectors/_fingerprint_card.html`, `connectors/_probe_alert.html`; route ordering `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/routes/connectors/__init__.py::build_router`.
- RBAC dependencies: `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/routes/connectors/operator.py:152` (`resolve_role_probe`, soft-hide), `:184` (`resolve_operator_or_403`, hard 403).
- Corpus surface to extend: `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/routes/corpus/routes.py:136` (`_resolve_operator`); empty-state template arm `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/templates/corpus/index.html` (final `{% else %}` block).
- CSRF: `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/csrf.py` (`mint_csrf_token`, `CSRF_COOKIE_NAME`).
- HTMX 2 `hx-post`/`hx-swap`/`hx-disabled-elt`/`HX-Redirect`: https://htmx.org/reference/ ; `hx-disabled-elt`: https://htmx.org/attributes/hx-disabled-elt/ . Vendored at `backend/src/meho_backplane/ui/templates/_head_assets.html:35,37`.
